issues.legal_issue: A second appeal governed by the continuing local appellate law need not be admitted or decided on a formulated substantial question of law.
material_facts: The case arose from Haryana and reached the High Court in a second appeal.
A pre-Constitution local law governing second appeals continued to apply in the relevant territory; that law did not require formulation of a substantial question of law.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not required to formulate a substantial question of law before deciding the second appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Section 41 of the Punjab Courts Act, 1918, rather than Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure as amended in 1976, governed second appeals in Haryana. The local law continued under Article 372(1) of the Constitution and remained applicable after the formation of Haryana under Sections 88 and 89 of the Punjab Re-organisation Act, 1966. The Constitution Bench decision in Pankajakshi v. Chandrika rejected the contrary reasoning in Kulwant Kaur v. Gurdial Singh Mann; Kirodi v. Ram Parkash followed Pankajakshi. Under the applicable local rule, formulation of a substantial question of law was unnecessary, although the second appeal remained confined to questions of law.

predicates.second_appeal: The matter came before the High Court as a second appeal from an appellate decree.
predicates.continuing_local_appeal_law_applies: A pre-existing local rule governing second appeals continued to govern appeals in the relevant jurisdiction.
predicates.local_appeal_law_does_not_require_substa: The continuing local rule did not require a substantial question of law to be formulated for the second appeal.

issues.definition: When a second appeal is governed by a continuing local rule that does not require a formulated substantial question of law, the appeal need not proceed on such a formulated question.

issues.legal_issue: In a second appeal, a claim to land cannot be granted merely because the opposing party did not make a counterclaim concerning that land when the claimant has failed to prove the claim on the evidence.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought declaration and possession of several plots on the basis that the defendants' tenancy had ended and that a defendant had sub-let the land.
The trial court and the first appellate court found that the plaintiffs had not proved their right to the land or the alleged sub-tenancy.
The High Court upheld those findings for the other plots but granted relief for two plots because the defendants had not made a counterclaim concerning them.
The defendants had generally denied the plaintiffs' claim, and the plaintiffs' claim for those two plots rested on the same grounds that the lower courts had found unproved.
issues.conclusion: The High Court's decree granting the plaintiffs relief for the two plots was erroneous and was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 41 of the Punjab Courts Act, 1918, a second appeal concerns questions of law and is not a forum to re-examine or re-appreciate facts settled by the trial and first appellate courts. A claimant must succeed on the strength of their own evidence; the absence of a counterclaim by the opposing party does not itself establish the claimant's case. Pankajakshi v. Chandrika and Kirodi v. Ram Parkash are relied on for the applicable second-appeal framework.

predicates.second_appeal: The matter is a second appeal from an appellate decree.
predicates.concurrent_finding_claimant_failed_to_pr: The trial court and the first appellate court found that the claimant had not proved entitlement to the disputed property.
predicates.relief_granted_only_because_opponent_mad: The second appellate court granted the claimant relief because the opponent had not counterclaimed concerning the property, rather than because the claimant proved the claim.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, if both lower courts found that the claimant failed to prove entitlement and relief was granted only because the opponent made no counterclaim, the unsupported decree must be set aside.

issues.legal_issue: A defendant may bring a counterclaim on an independent cause of action, but the counterclaim must be against the plaintiff and cannot concern property on which the plaintiff made no claim.
material_facts: The plaintiffs' suit described and claimed rights in specified plots but made no claim concerning two other plots.
The defendant included those two other plots in a counterclaim, and the trial court and first appellate court allowed that counterclaim.
The High Court rejected the counterclaim because it did not concern any claim made by the plaintiffs.
issues.conclusion: The High Court correctly rejected the counterclaim concerning the two plots that were not part of the plaintiffs' claim.
issues.legal_principle: Order VIII, Rule 6A of the Code of Civil Procedure permits a counterclaim, including one based on an independent cause of action, but requires it to be against the plaintiff. A counterclaim unrelated to any claim made by the plaintiff is not permitted; the court also observed that it should have been excluded under Order VIII, Rule 6C. Jag Mohan Chawla v. Dera Radha Swami Satsang establishes that an independent cause of action may support a counterclaim, subject to the requirement that it be against the plaintiff.

predicates.civil_suit: The dispute is a civil suit in which the defendant has an opportunity to plead a counterclaim.
predicates.defendant_counterclaims_for_property: The defendant seeks affirmative relief concerning property through a counterclaim.
predicates.plaintiff_made_no_claim_concerning_that_: The plaintiff's suit does not assert any right or seek relief concerning the property that is the subject of the counterclaim.

issues.definition: In a civil suit, a defendant's counterclaim for property is not maintainable when the plaintiff made no claim concerning that property.
